enrichment.short_title: CCE v Federation of Technological Industries: ECJ reference on VAT anti-abuse powers
key_facts: Mobile phone and computer traders challenged UK anti-abuse VAT provisions introduced to combat carousel and acquisition fraud costing billions annually.

Sections 17 and 18 of the Finance Act 2003 amended the VAT Act 1994 to create security and joint-and-several liability powers exercisable where traders knew or had reasonable grounds to suspect unpaid VAT.
Lightman J granted permission for judicial review and referred questions to the ECJ; CCE appealed the reference decision, not the grant of permission.
Jacob LJ held Article 21.3 acte clair conferred the necessary power, but Ward and Mantell LJJ doubted and the court maintained the ECJ reference.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Lightman J's decision to refer VAT anti-abuse questions to the ECJ following permission for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; court held it had jurisdiction to review the reference decision; majority maintained the ECJ reference with proposed questions despite Jacob LJ's view the point was acte clair.
enrichment.ratio: A national court of appeal may review whether a first instance judge was right to refer under Article 234 EC Treaty; whether Article 21.3 permits general joint-and-several liability to combat VAT abuse was not acte clair where purposive construction and legislative history remained arguable.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal may interfere with a decision to refer questions to the ECJ
Whether Article 21.3 of the Sixth VAT Directive confers a general power to impose joint and several liability subject only to general principles
Whether the security and joint-and-several provisions were proportionate anti-abuse measures
Whether the point was acte clair so that no reference was necessary
linked_authorities: R v International Stock Exchange ex parte Else [1993] QB 534
Bulmer v Bollinger [1974] 1 Ch 401
Rheinmuhlen-Dusseldorf v Einfuhr und Vorratsstelle Getreide Case 166/73

enrichment.short_title: Borak v SSHD: section 96(2) certification of fresh asylum claim
key_facts: Croatian claimant of Serbian ethnicity failed asylum and human rights appeals based on fear of return and family killings linked to General Gotovina's indictment.

After further representations treated as a fresh asylum claim, the Secretary of State refused the claim and certified it under section 96(2) as relying on grounds already raised or required in earlier appeals.
The claimant argued asylum and Article 3 human rights grounds were distinct legal creatures so certification under section 96(2)(a) was unlawful.
Permission was limited by Buxton LJ so the claimant proceeded on the basis of no substantial factual difference between the fresh claim and the human rights appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a section 96(2) certificate preventing appeal against refusal of a fresh asylum claim; permission granted on a restricted basis.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Harrison J held a purposive reading of 'ground' permitted certification where factual and legal issues were substantially the same despite different legal labels, and section 96(2)(b) also applied; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: For section 96(2) certification 'ground' comprises factual and legal aspects akin to a cause of action; where asylum and Article 3 claims raise the same substantive risk and protection issues, differing legal frameworks do not prevent certification designed to achieve finality.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'ground' in section 96(2) of the 2002 Act
Whether an asylum ground is distinct from an Article 3 human rights ground for certification purposes
Application of section 96(2)(b) where indictment evidence existed at the time of the one-stop statement
Whether certification should follow a purposive or technical approach

enrichment.short_title: MMR vaccine group litigation: case management after legal aid withdrawal
key_facts: Large group litigation alleging MMR/MR vaccine damage faced collapse after the Legal Services Commission withdrew funding for lead and non-lead claimants.
Claimants divided between those discontinuing, those awaiting possible funding restoration, those proceeding privately, and 110 who had not stated intentions.
Defendants offered costs amnesties for discontinuance or dismissal; many parents lacked legal advice on limitation, costs exposure, and funding prospects.
Keith J made directions on notification deadlines, expert report disclosure for FRC appeals, and gave in-principle approval to defendants' settlement terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management conference in ongoing group litigation following withdrawal of public funding.
enrichment.outcome: Orders made requiring undecided claimants to notify intentions by 22 October 2004 or face dismissal; discontinuance deadlines extended; expert materials disclosed for funding appeals; court approved settlement terms in principle for SmithKline, APMSD and Merck.
enrichment.ratio: Where public funding ends in mass tort litigation, the court may impose notification sanctions and extend deadlines to allow funding appeals to conclude, while approving costs-amnesty settlements only after balancing limitation, res judicata, and future claim risks for disabled child claimants.
legal_issues: Appropriate sanctions for claimants failing to notify intentions to proceed or discontinue
Whether group litigation status could be terminated without the Lord Chief Justice revoking the practice direction
Effect of discontinuance versus dismissal on limitation and future negligence claims
Whether prospective cost-capping orders were justified
Court's power to approve settlements for persons under disability under CPR 21.10

enrichment.short_title: Skanska v Egger: quantum assessment after GMP contract dispute
key_facts: Following a May 2002 liability judgment, the court assessed quantum on hundreds of disputed items under a guaranteed maximum price contract between Egger and Skanska (successor to Kvaerner).
Major claims included removal of spoil, acceleration costs, consequential warehouse and transport losses, professional fees, and rectification of the fire fighting system.
Quantum experts Wishart and Simper narrowed many items; structural experts Masterton and Walsh assisted on technical valuations.
Individual claim valuations were determined throughout the judgment; final sums depended on complex agreed interest formulations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court quantum trial read with the earlier liability judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Individual claim and counterclaim items valued in detail throughout the judgment; several Egger counterclaim items rejected or substantially reduced; parties to reflect agreed interest calculations in the final judgment sum.
enrichment.ratio: Quantum in complex construction disputes should be resolved item-by-item with expert assistance; costs claimed must be substantiated by contemporary evidence and represent genuine professional or contractual entitlement rather than litigation support work.
legal_issues: Valuation of spoil removal and site availability claims
Recoverability of acceleration agreement costs
Assessment of consequential warehouse and logistics losses
Whether professional and WSP fees were contract administration or recoverable damages
Rectification costs for the fire fighting system

enrichment.short_title: Gleave v Holder: permission refused on classic motorcycle auction fraud
key_facts: Buyer Holder rescinded an auction purchase of a 1964 Aermacchi racing motorcycle after discovering it was mainly a 1970-71 road model with mismatched numbers.
HHJ Cowell found seller Gleave fraudulently misrepresented the year, authenticity of numbers, and racing character, rejecting reliance on auction conditions.
Expert Linton testified he told Gleave before the auction the description was false; joint expert Bladon confirmed the misrepresentations.
Gleave sought permission to appeal and to add late evidence from Italian dealer Altinier that he had described the bike as 1964/65 when selling to Gleave.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from county court judgment for fraudulent misrepresentation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal dismissed; Potter and Arden LJJ upheld trial judge's fraud findings on circa 1964 and crankcase number representations and rejected challenges to exclusion of late Altinier evidence and joint expert procedure.
enrichment.ratio: Findings of deliberate or reckless misrepresentation at trial are highly resistant to appeal; late witness evidence on central fraud issues should be excluded where not sought before trial, and joint expert reports may be relied on without oral evidence unless bias is substantiated.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in excluding a single additional question to witness Altinier
Admissibility of fresh Altinier evidence on appeal under Ladd v Marshall
Propriety of relying on joint expert written reports after pre-trial conference with one party
Whether auction conditions excluded liability for fraudulent misrepresentation
linked_authorities: Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337
Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

enrichment.short_title: Guveya v NASS: Hard Cases support refused for failed Zimbabwe claimant
key_facts: Zimbabwe national Guveya failed asylum with all appeals exhausted and NASS section 95 support terminated.
He sought Hard Cases support under section 4 after the Home Office maintained a policy of not enforcing removal to Zimbabwe while expecting voluntary return.
The claimant argued the non-enforcement policy made voluntary return unreasonable and that refusal breached Article 3 positive obligations.
Interim relief had kept him in accommodation pending this judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of NASS refusal of section 4 Hard Cases support and accommodation.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Moses J held the Secretary of State could expect voluntary return despite non-enforcement policy, section 4 was not engaged, and absence of support did not constitute Article 3 'treatment'; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A policy suspending enforced removal to Zimbabwe on political rather than safety grounds does not make refusal of voluntary return unreasonable or require Hard Cases support; section 4 protects those unable to leave, not those choosing to remain destitute; withholding support is not Convention 'treatment'.
legal_issues: Whether non-enforcement of removal to Zimbabwe rendered voluntary return unreasonable
Correct application of the Hard Cases support policy under section 4
Whether section 4 provides a safety net analogous to non-removal policy
Whether refusal of support engages Article 3 positive obligations under Limbuela principles

enrichment.short_title: Hussain v SSHD: Article 8 removal of illegal entrant spouse
key_facts: Pakistani citizen entered the UK illegally in 1995 and married a British citizen with four stepchildren in 1999.
A consultant psychiatrist reported removal would cause psychological harm because the applicant had become a father figure after a prior kidnapping trauma.
The Special Adjudicator held out-of-country entry clearance would be disproportionate under Article 8; the IAT reversed, emphasising immigration history and effective control.
The IAT treated removal as a temporary interference because the applicant could apply from Pakistan within about six months.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from IAT decision restoring the Secretary of State's removal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; Tuckey and Potter LJJ held the IAT legitimately balanced effective immigration control against family life and had considered impact on wife and stepchildren.
enrichment.ratio: Section 65(1) requires primary focus on the appellant's own Article 8 rights; an illegal entrant's marriage does not queue-jump immigration procedures, and temporary separation for out-of-country entry clearance can be justified where family reunification remains achievable.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT could interfere with the Special Adjudicator's Article 8 assessment after Subesh
Extent to which impact on stepchildren should be considered
Whether requiring out-of-country entry clearance was a disproportionate Article 8 interference
Relevance of the applicant's illegal entry and immigration history
linked_authorities: Subesh v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 56

enrichment.short_title: T v T: summary assessment of father's costs after USA trip dispute
key_facts: Father applied for permission to take his 10-year-old son to the USA for Easter 2004; mother opposed but the dispute settled on undertakings about travel frequency.
The court had ordered the mother to pay half the father's costs; the father claimed £8,481 including VAT.
The mother, acting in person, challenged the costs as disproportionate; The Costs Partnership suggested £4,254 was appropriate.
The judge conducted a summary assessment rather than detailed assessment to avoid further expense on a straightforward order-interpretation application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written submissions on quantum following an earlier costs order in settled children proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Father's recoverable costs from the mother assessed at £5,000 total, so she pays £2,500 as one half; figure reduced for disproportionate fee earner rates and unnecessary counsel work.
enrichment.ratio: On summary assessment of costs in short one-day family applications, the paying party should only bear sums proportionately and reasonably incurred; senior fee earners and counsel advice may be excessive where solicitors could settle a simple order-interpretation dispute.
legal_issues: Whether summary or detailed assessment was appropriate
What costs were proportionate for a settled holiday contact application
Application of CPR 44.5 conduct and proportionality factors
Extent to which the mother's liability should reflect senior solicitor and counsel charges

enrichment.short_title: R v Coates and others: jurisdiction after death of Court of Appeal judge
key_facts: Appeals against conviction heard by Kay LJ, Evans J and Pitchers J were reserved after full argument.
The three judges met and agreed outcomes and reasons, but Kay LJ died before drafting the judgment.
Counsel argued the remaining two judges lacked jurisdiction to determine convictions under section 55 because appeals were not finally 'determined'.
Kay LJ had announced in open court dismissal of some renewed leave applications in the Terry appeal before his death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary hearing on whether the Court of Appeal Criminal Division could give judgment after the presiding judge's death.
enrichment.outcome: Reserved conviction appeals not determined and must be reheard before a fresh three-judge court; decisions announced in open court before death remain valid and reasons may be given by surviving judges; sentence appeals to follow rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 55 SCA 1981 an appeal against conviction is not determined until the court's decision is binding on its members, so provisional agreement before draft judgment does not suffice; but an oral announcement of allow/dismiss at the hearing is a final determination surviving a judge's later death.
legal_issues: When an appeal against conviction is 'determined' for section 55 purposes
Whether surviving judges may deliver reasons for an orally announced decision
Effect of Kay LJ's death on reserved judgments versus announced decisions
Consequential listing and constitution directions for rehearing

enrichment.short_title: Maden v Cliffords: overlapping solicitor negligence and loss of chance
key_facts: Maden bought development land negligently searched by Goodwin solicitors, then faced Wardle adverse possession claim over valuable Plot A advised by Cliffords.
Goodwin paid £100,000 in May 1996 to settle the conveyancing negligence claim; Cliffords wrongly advised payments into court protected against adverse costs in the Wardle action.
The trial judge found Maden would have settled the Wardle action for £20,000 plus costs by 30 September 1996 if properly advised; Chadburn ultimately won Plot A at trial.
Cliffords appealed arguing double recovery from the Goodwin settlement and that damages should be discounted for settlement uncertainty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court award of damages against Cliffords for negligent costs advice in adverse possession litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court rejected double recovery argument but applied a 20% Allied Maples discount because Mrs Chadburn's willingness to settle at £20,000 was high but not certain.
enrichment.ratio: Where successive negligent solicitors cause distinct losses at different times, an earlier settlement with one firm does not reduce damages for a later novus actus by another; loss-of-chance principles require discounting unless the counterparty's acceptance of settlement was virtually certain.
legal_issues: Whether Goodwin settlement precluded recovery against Cliffords for later Wardle action losses
Admissibility of evidence as to how the Goodwin settlement figure was composed
Proper discount for uncertainty of Mrs Chadburn accepting a £20,000 settlement
Application of Allied Maples loss-of-chance principles to solicitor negligence
linked_authorities: Allied Maples Group Ltd v Simmons & Simmons [1995] 1 WLR 1602
Ford v White & Co [1964] 1 WLR 885
Cottrill v Steyning & Littlehampton Building Society [1966] 1 WLR 753
